title: The Balance Sheet Equation
context: Review how the balance sheet equation requires total assets to equal total liabilities plus total equity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: An office computer kept in service by an operating business for more than one year is classified as a non-current tangible asset.
An office computer held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as inventory, a current asset, rather than as a non-current asset.
The same office computer may be a non-current asset for one business and inventory for another, depending on whether it is used or held for sale.
Classifying an office computer as a non-current asset depends on management's intention to use it in operations rather than to sell it quickly.
When an office computer is purchased to be resold rather than used, it belongs among current assets as inventory.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Continued use beyond one year by the business itself makes the office computer a non-current tangible asset.
TRUE — Held for resale rather than use, the office computer counts as inventory under current assets.
TRUE — Intended use versus resale, not physical form, decides whether the office computer is non-current or current.
TRUE — Intention to use over the long term is the deciding factor for non-current classification of the office computer.
TRUE — Resale intent places the office computer in inventory, a current asset category.

title: Balance Sheet as a Point-in-Time Snapshot
context: Review the balance sheet as a snapshot of a business's assets, equity and liabilities on one specific date. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A financial statement typically brings together a balance sheet, a statement of profit and loss, and a cash flow statement to describe a business's position, performance and cash movements.

Revenue earned and costs incurred over an accounting period are reported in the statement of profit and loss rather than in the balance sheet.
Depreciation reflects the gradual wearing out of a fixed asset as it is used to generate revenue over its useful life.
A fixed asset that is never depreciated would remain on the accounts at its original cost even after years of use, overstating its true worth.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — These three statements together describe financial position, trading performance and cash movements more fully than any one alone.
TRUE — Only the balance sheet is a snapshot on one date; the other two statements summarise activity across an accounting period.
TRUE — The statement of profit and loss, not the balance sheet, records revenue and costs accumulated over the period.
TRUE — Depreciation allocates the loss of value that a fixed asset experiences through use over its useful life.
TRUE — Without depreciation, an asset stays at original cost in the accounts despite having lost value through use, which overstates it.

Revenue earned and costs incurred over an accounting period are reported in the balance sheet rather than in the statement of profit and loss.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Depreciation is a non-cash expense; the related cash was paid when the asset was originally bought, not when the charge is recorded.
FALSE — A financial statement normally includes a balance sheet, a statement of profit and loss and a cash flow statement together.
TRUE — Straight-line depreciation charges the same amount every year of useful life, producing a steady annual fall in book value.
FALSE — The balance sheet is drawn up at a single point in time; it is the other two statements that cover a period.
FALSE — Revenue and costs for the period are reported in the statement of profit and loss, not the balance sheet.

title: Cash Flow From Operating Activities
context: Analyze why the statement of profit and loss covers a period rather than a single point in time. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

FALSE — Depreciation is a non-cash expense; it does not itself trigger a cash payment in the year it is recorded.

title: Reading Financial Statements Cautiously in Practice
context: Analyze how a single year's balance sheet or income statement can be misleading without wider context. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A single year's balance sheet or income statement rarely tells the full story about a business, so the figures are best interpreted alongside additional context rather than read in isolation.

Because published financial statements condense complex operations into a handful of line items, readers should interpret the figures cautiously rather than draw firm conclusions from any single number.
A single year's balance sheet or income statement always tells the full story about a business, so no other years or comparisons are ever needed.
A rise in profit for the year does not by itself prove that a business is being managed well, since the improvement could stem from a one-off item rather than from the core operations.
Because financial statements present exact figures, readers never need to interpret them cautiously or look for additional explanation.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Figures from one year alone lack context, so readers should look beyond a single year before drawing conclusions.
